imc-2007-01.title: Evaluate at $0,\pm1$
imc-2007-01.body:
Let $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. Then $5$ divides
$$f(0)=c,\qquad f(1)+f(-1)-2f(0)=2a,\qquad f(1)-f(-1)=2b .$$
Since $\gcd(2,5)=1$, $5$ divides $a$, $b$ and $c$. ∎

imc-2007-01.title: Count roots modulo 5
imc-2007-01.body: Reduce the coefficients modulo $5$ and regard $\bar f$ as a polynomial over the field $\mathbb F_5$. By hypothesis every element of $\mathbb F_5$ is a root of $\bar f$, so $\bar f$ has $5$ roots. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most $2$ over a field has at most $2$ roots, hence $\bar f=0$, i.e. all coefficients of $f$ are divisible by $5$. ∎

imc-2007-02.title: A $2	imes2$ minor, an explicit rank-2 matrix and a parity argument
imc-2007-02.body:
**The rank is at least 2.** Permuting rows and columns does not change the rank, so we may assume the entry $1$ is $a_{11}$, the first column is increasing ($a_{11}<a_{21}<\dots<a_{n1}$) and the first row is increasing ($a_{11}<a_{12}<\dots<a_{1n}$). The first column consists of $n$ distinct positive integers, so $a_{n1}\ge n$; similarly $a_{1n}\ge n$. They are different entries, so not both equal $n$; hence $a_{n1}a_{1n}>n^2\ge a_{nn}$ and
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{1n}\\a_{n1}&a_{nn}\end{pmatrix}=a_{nn}-a_{1n}a_{n1}<0 .$$
A nonzero $2\times2$ minor shows $\operatorname{rk}A\ge2$.

**Rank 2 is attained.** Let $T$ have entries $t_{ij}=(i-1)n+j$. Row $i$ equals $(1,2,\dots,n)+(i-1)n(1,1,\dots,1)$, so all rows lie in the span of two vectors and $\operatorname{rk}T\le2$; by the first part $\operatorname{rk}T=2$.

**Rank $n$ is attained.** Put odd numbers on the diagonal (there are $\lceil n^2/2\rceil\ge n$ odd numbers available), even numbers above the diagonal (we need $\frac{n(n-1)}2\le\lfloor n^2/2\rfloor$ of them), and the remaining numbers below the diagonal in any order. Modulo $2$ the matrix is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal, so its determinant is odd, in particular nonzero, and the rank is $n$.

**Answer:** minimal rank $2$, maximal rank $n$. ∎

imc-2007-03.title: Constructions for $k\le2$, first columns for $k\ge3$
imc-2007-03.body:
**Answer:** $k=1$ and $k=2$.

**$k=1$:** $P(x)=\alpha x^2=\det(xA_1)$ with $A_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\alpha\end{pmatrix}$.

**$k=2$:** $P(x,y)=\alpha x^2+\gamma xy+\beta y^2$. With $A_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\alpha\end{pmatrix}$, $A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\-1&\gamma\end{pmatrix}$,
$$\det(xA_1+yA_2)=\det\begin{pmatrix}x&\beta y\\-y&\alpha x+\gamma y\end{pmatrix}=x(\alpha x+\gamma y)+\beta y^2=P(x,y).$$

**$k\ge3$:** we show $P=x_1^2+\dots+x_k^2$ is not good. Suppose $P=\det\bigl(\sum x_iA_i\bigr)$. The first columns of $A_1,\dots,A_k$ are $k\ge3$ vectors in $\mathbb R^2$, hence linearly dependent: there is $(y_1,\dots,y_k)\ne0$ such that $\sum y_iA_i$ has zero first column. Then $\det\bigl(\sum y_iA_i\bigr)=0$, while $P(y_1,\dots,y_k)=\sum y_i^2>0$ — a contradiction. ∎

imc-2007-04.title: Three counting rules
imc-2007-04.body:
We use three simple facts, for arbitrary $U,V,W\subseteq G$.

1. $N_{UVG}=|U|\cdot|V|$: for each $x\in U$, $y\in V$ there is exactly one $z\in G$ with $xyz=e$, namely $z=(xy)^{-1}$.
2. $N_{UVW}=N_{VWU}=N_{WUV}$: $xyz=e\iff yzx=e$ (conjugate by $x$), so $(x,y,z)\mapsto(y,z,x)$ is a bijection between the triples counted by $N_{UVW}$ and by $N_{VWU}$.
3. If $W$ is the disjoint union of $W_1,W_2,W_3$, then $N_{UVW}=N_{UVW_1}+N_{UVW_2}+N_{UVW_3}$.

Now, using 3, then 1 and 2, then 1 and 3 again, and finally 2:
$$N_{ABC}=N_{ABG}-N_{ABA}-N_{ABB}=|A||B|-N_{BAA}-N_{BAB}=N_{BAG}-N_{BAA}-N_{BAB}=N_{BAC}=N_{CBA}.$$
(Here $N_{ABA}=N_{BAA}$ and $N_{ABB}=N_{BAB}$ are cyclic shifts, and $N_{BAC}=N_{ACB}=N_{CBA}$.) ∎

imc-2007-05.title: An ideal of polynomials
imc-2007-05.body:
**Normalisation.** Let $a=\min_ia_i$. Replacing $k$ by $k-a\ell$ (which runs over all integers as $k$ does) the condition becomes $\sum_if(k+(a_i-a)\ell)=0$, so we may assume all $a_i\ge0$.

**The ideal.** Let
$$I=\Bigl\{P(X)=\sum_{j=0}^mb_jX^j\in\mathbb R[X]:\ \sum_{j=0}^mb_jf(k+j\ell)=0\ \text{for all }k,\ell\in\mathbb Z,\ \ell\neq0\Bigr\}.$$
It is a linear subspace. If $P\in I$ then $XP\in I$, since $\sum b_jf(k+(j+1)\ell)=\sum b_jf((k+\ell)+j\ell)=0$. So $I$ is an ideal, and it contains $R(X)=\sum_{i=1}^nX^{a_i}$, so $I\ne0$. Two more properties:

- *$P(X)\in I\Rightarrow P(X^m)\in I$ for $m\ge1$*: $\sum b_jf(k+jm\ell)=0$ is the defining condition with $\ell$ replaced by $m\ell\neq0$.
- *If $P\in I$ and $P(0)=0$, then $P/X\in I$*: if $P=\sum_{j\ge1}b_jX^j$, then $\sum_{j\ge0}b_{j+1}f(k+j\ell)=\sum_{j\ge1}b_jf((k-\ell)+j\ell)=0$.

$\mathbb R[X]$ is a principal ideal domain, so $I=(Q)$ for some $Q\neq0$. By the last property $Q(0)\ne0$ (otherwise $Q/X\in I$ would be a nonzero element of smaller degree, not divisible by $Q$).

**Conclusion.** If $Q$ is a nonzero constant, then $1\in I$, which says exactly $f(k)=0$ for all $k$. Suppose instead $Q$ has a complex root $c$; then $c\ne0$. For every $m\ge1$, $Q(X^m)\in I$, so $Q(X)\mid Q(X^m)$ and $Q(c^m)=0$. As $Q$ has finitely many roots, $c^i=c^j$ for some $i<j$, so $c^N=1$ with $N=j-i\ge1$, and therefore $Q(1)=Q(c^N)=0$. Then every $P\in I$ satisfies $P(1)=0$; but $R(1)=n\ne0$. This contradiction shows $Q$ is constant, so $f=0$. ∎

imc-2007-06.title: Average over roots of unity
imc-2007-06.body:
**Answer:** $0$, $1$ or $2$.

All three are possible: $P_0=0$, $P_1=1$, $P_2=1+z$ (note $|1+z|\le2$ on $|z|=1$).

Now let $P$ satisfy the conditions and have at least two nonzero coefficients. Dividing by a power of $z$ (which does not change $|P|$ on the unit circle) and possibly replacing $P$ by $-P$, we may assume $P(z)=a_0+a_1z+\dots+a_nz^n$ with $n\ge1$, $a_0>0$ and $a_n\ne0$. Let $Q(z)=a_1z+\dots+a_{n-1}z^{n-1}$.

Choose $w_0$ on the unit circle with $a_nw_0^n=|a_n|$ (i.e. $w_0^n=\pm1$ according to the sign of $a_n$) and let $w_k=w_0\varepsilon^k$, $k=0,\dots,n-1$, with $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/n}$. These are $n$ distinct points with $a_nw_k^n=|a_n|$. For $1\le j\le n-1$, $\sum_kw_k^j=w_0^j\sum_k\varepsilon^{jk}=0$, hence $\sum_kQ(w_k)=0$ and
$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}P(w_k)=a_0+|a_n|\ge2,$$
since $a_0,|a_n|$ are positive integers. On the other hand $\operatorname{Re}P(w_k)\le|P(w_k)|\le2$ for each $k$. An average of numbers $\le2$ equals $\ge2$ only if all equal $2$: so $\operatorname{Re}P(w_k)=2=|P(w_k)|$, i.e. $P(w_k)=2$ for every $k$, and $a_0=|a_n|=1$. Then $Q(w_k)=P(w_k)-a_0-a_nw_k^n=2-1-1=0$ for all $k$. So $Q$, of degree at most $n-1$, has $n$ distinct roots: $Q=0$. Hence $P=a_0+a_nz^n$ has exactly two nonzero coefficients.

*Remark.* Parseval's identity $\sum|a_j|^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|P(e^{it})|^2dt\le4$ quickly shows there are at most $4$ nonzero coefficients, all $\pm1$ when there are at least two, but it does not by itself exclude $1\pm z^m\pm z^n$. ∎

imc-2007-07.title: A counterexample: the exponential
imc-2007-07.body:
**Answer: No.**

Take $f(x)=e^x$, which is continuous and not of the form $ax+b$. For $c>0$,
$$cf(x)=ce^x=e^{x+\ln c}=f(x+\ln c),$$
so the graph of $cf$ is the graph of $f$ translated horizontally by $-\ln c$. Thus $f$ has the property but is not linear. ∎

imc-2007-08.title: List the fourth powers modulo 29
imc-2007-08.body:
We show $29$ divides each of $x,y,z$; then $29^4$ divides each of $x^4,y^4,z^4$ and hence $S$.

Suppose not; by symmetry $29\nmid x$. Since $\mathbb Z/29$ is a field, choose $w$ with $xw\equiv1\pmod{29}$; multiplying by $w^4$, the numbers $xw,yw,zw$ also have fourth-power sum divisible by $29$. So we may assume $x\equiv1$ and must rule out
$$1+y^4+z^4\equiv0\pmod{29}.$$

**Fourth powers mod 29.** The group $(\mathbb Z/29)^\times$ is cyclic of order $28$, so the nonzero fourth powers form its subgroup of order $28/4=7$. Computing, $1^4=1$, $2^4=16$, $3^4=81\equiv23$, $4^4=256\equiv24$, $6^4=1296\equiv20$, $8^4=4096\equiv7$, $11^4=14641\equiv25$; so the fourth powers mod $29$ are
$$F=\{0,1,7,16,20,23,24,25\}.$$
We need $y^4\equiv-1-z^4$ with $z^4\in F$. The values $-1-t$ for $t\in F$ are
$$28,\ 27,\ 21,\ 12,\ 8,\ 5,\ 4,\ 3\pmod{29},$$
none of which is in $F$. So the congruence is impossible, a contradiction. ∎

imc-2007-09.title: Iterate from the minimum
imc-2007-09.body:
Since $C$ is closed, bounded and nonempty, $a=\min C$ exists and $C\subseteq[a,b]$ with $b=\max C$. Define $x_0=a$ and $x_{k+1}=f(x_k)\in C$.

We have $x_1=f(a)\ge a=x_0$ because $f(a)\in C$. If $x_{k+1}\ge x_k$, then, $f$ being nondecreasing, $x_{k+2}=f(x_{k+1})\ge f(x_k)=x_{k+1}$. So $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing and bounded by $b$, hence converges to some $L$; $L\in C$ because $C$ is closed. By continuity of $f$ on $C$,
$$f(L)=\lim f(x_k)=\lim x_{k+1}=L .$$
So $p=L$ is a fixed point. ∎

imc-2007-09.title: Supremum argument (official)
imc-2007-09.body:
Suppose $f(x)\ne x$ for all $x\in C$. Let $a=\min C$, $b=\max C$ (they exist since $C$ is closed and bounded). As $f(a),f(b)\in C$, we get $f(a)>a$ and $f(b)<b$.

Let $p=\sup\{x\in C:f(x)>x\}$; the set contains $a$, and $p\in C$ since $C$ is closed. There are $x_k\in C$ with $f(x_k)>x_k$ and $x_k\to p$, so by continuity $f(p)\ge p$, hence $f(p)>p$. Every $x\in C$ with $x>p$ satisfies $f(x)<x$ (by definition of $p$ and the assumption). In particular $q=f(p)\in C$ satisfies $q>p$, so $f(q)<q=f(p)$. But $p<q$ and $f$ nondecreasing give $f(p)\le f(q)$ — a contradiction. ∎

imc-2007-10.title: Circulant eigenvalues
imc-2007-10.body:
Let $P$ be the cyclic permutation matrix with $Pe_j=e_{j+1}$ (indices mod $n$). Then $A=2I+P^2+P^{-2}$ (for $n=3$ the entries $\pm2$ coincide with $\mp1$, and the formula still describes $A$). $P$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues $\omega^k$, $k=0,\dots,n-1$, where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$; so the eigenvalues of $A$ are
$$2+\omega^{2k}+\omega^{-2k}=|1+\omega^{2k}|^2 .$$
Since $n$ is odd, $k\mapsto2k$ permutes the residues mod $n$, so
$$\det A=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}|1+\omega^k|^2=\Bigl|\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1+\omega^k)\Bigr|^2 .$$
From $\prod_k(x-\omega^k)=x^n-1$ at $x=-1$: $(-1)^n\prod_k(1+\omega^k)=(-1)^n-1=-2$, so $\prod_k(1+\omega^k)=2$ ($n$ odd). Hence $\det A=4$.

**Answer: 4**

imc-2007-10.title: Write $A$ as a square
imc-2007-10.body:
Let $B$ be the adjacency matrix of the $n$-cycle: $b_{ij}=1$ if $i-j\equiv\pm1\pmod n$, else $0$. Then $(B^2)_{ij}$ is the number of common neighbours of $i$ and $j$ in the cycle: $2$ if $i=j$, $1$ if $i-j\equiv\pm2$, and $0$ otherwise (for $n=3$, $\pm2\equiv\mp1$ and adjacent vertices have one common neighbour). So $A=B^2$ and $\det A=(\det B)^2$.

With the shift $P$ as in the first solution, $B=P+P^{-1}=P^{-1}(P^2+I)$. $\det P=\operatorname{sgn}(n\text{-cycle})=(-1)^{n-1}=1$. Since $n$ is odd, $P^2$ is again the matrix of an $n$-cycle, with characteristic polynomial $\det(xI-P^2)=x^n-1$. At $x=-1$: $\det(-I-P^2)=(-1)^n-1=-2$, so $\det(I+P^2)=(-1)^n\cdot(-2)=2$. Therefore $\det B=2$ and $\det A=4$.

**Answer: 4**

imc-2007-11.title: Exterior-algebra construction and independent vectors
imc-2007-11.body:
**Answer:** $n_k=2^k$.

**Construction for $n=2^k$.** Let $V$ have basis vectors $e_S$ indexed by the subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$, and define
$$A_ie_S=\begin{cases}e_{S\cup\{i\}}&i\notin S,\\0&i\in S.\end{cases}$$
Then $A_i^2e_S=0$ (after one application $i$ is in the set), and for $i\neq j$ both $A_iA_je_S$ and $A_jA_ie_S$ equal $e_{S\cup\{i,j\}}$ if $i,j\notin S$ and $0$ otherwise, so the $A_i$ commute. Finally $A_1A_2\cdots A_ke_\varnothing=e_{\{1,\dots,k\}}\ne0$. (Equivalently, $A_i=I\otimes\cdots\otimes N\otimes\cdots\otimes I$ with $N=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ in the $i$-th slot.)

**Lower bound.** Let $A_1,\dots,A_k$ be $n\times n$ matrices with the three properties, and pick $v$ with $A_1\cdots A_kv\ne0$. For $X\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$ let $A_X=\prod_{i\in X}A_i$ (order irrelevant by commutativity) and $v_X=A_Xv$. We claim the $2^k$ vectors $v_X$ are linearly independent; then $n\ge2^k$.

Suppose $\sum_X\lambda_Xv_X=0$ with not all $\lambda_X=0$, and choose $X_0$ with $\lambda_{X_0}\neq0$ and $|X_0|$ minimal. Let $\bar X_0$ be the complement of $X_0$ and apply $A_{\bar X_0}$. If $X\not\subseteq X_0$, then some $i\in X\cap\bar X_0$, and $A_{\bar X_0}A_X$ contains the factor $A_i^2=0$, so $A_{\bar X_0}v_X=0$. If $X\subseteq X_0$ and $\lambda_X\ne0$, minimality forces $X=X_0$. Hence
$$0=\lambda_{X_0}A_{\bar X_0}A_{X_0}v=\lambda_{X_0}A_1A_2\cdots A_kv,$$
so $\lambda_{X_0}=0$, a contradiction. ∎

imc-2007-12.title: Rescale around $x=-n$: a Hermite limit
imc-2007-12.body:
Let $m=\deg f$ and divide $f$ by its leading coefficient (this changes no roots, and $f_n$ is linear in $f$), so $f$ is monic. If $m=0$ there is nothing to prove, so let $m\ge1$. Note $f_n$ is monic of degree $m$ for every $n$.

**Operators on $\mathcal P_m$.** Let $\mathcal P_m$ be the space of real polynomials of degree $\le m$ and $D$ the derivative; $D^{m+1}=0$ on $\mathcal P_m$, so every power series in $D$ is a finite sum (a polynomial in $D$), and the usual formal identities hold. In particular, with $L(D)=\log(1+D)-D=\sum_{j=2}^m\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}D^j$,
$$f_n=(1+D)^nf=e^{n\log(1+D)}f=e^{nD}\,e^{nL(D)}f .$$
By Taylor's formula $e^{nD}g(x)=g(x+n)$, so $f_n(x)=h_n(x+n)$ with $h_n=e^{nL(D)}f$. It suffices to show that $h_n$ has only real roots for large $n$.

**Rescaling.** Define $H_n(t)=n^{-m/2}h_n(\sqrt n\,t)$. If $(\sigma g)(t)=g(\sqrt nt)$, then $\sigma(Dg)=n^{-1/2}D(\sigma g)$, hence $\sigma\,p(D)=p(n^{-1/2}D)\,\sigma$ for every polynomial $p$, and
$$H_n=\exp\Bigl(nL(n^{-1/2}D)\Bigr)g_n,\qquad g_n(t)=n^{-m/2}f(\sqrt nt).$$
Now $nL(n^{-1/2}D)=-\frac{D^2}2+\sum_{j=3}^m\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}n^{1-j/2}D^j\to-\frac{D^2}{2}$, and $g_n(t)=t^m+\sum_{j<m}c_jn^{(j-m)/2}t^j\to t^m$ (where $f=x^m+\sum_{j<m}c_jx^j$). Since everything happens in the finite-dimensional space $\mathcal P_m$ and $\exp$ is continuous there, $H_n\to p_m:=e^{-D^2/2}t^m$ coefficientwise. Each $H_n$ is monic of degree $m$.

**$p_m$ has $m$ simple real roots.** Here $t$ denotes multiplication by $t$. From $D^{2r}t=tD^{2r}+2rD^{2r-1}$ (Leibniz rule),
$$e^{-D^2/2}t=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{(-1/2)^r}{r!}\bigl(tD^{2r}+2rD^{2r-1}\bigr)=t\,e^{-D^2/2}-D\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{(-1/2)^{r-1}}{(r-1)!}D^{2r-2}=(t-D)\,e^{-D^2/2}.$$ Hence $p_0=1$ and $p_{m+1}=(t-D)p_m=tp_m-p_m'$. Note
$$tp_m(t)-p_m'(t)=-e^{t^2/2}\bigl(e^{-t^2/2}p_m(t)\bigr)'.$$
Suppose $p_m$ has $m$ simple real roots $r_1<\dots<r_m$ (true for $m=1$: $p_1=t$). The function $G=e^{-t^2/2}p_m$ vanishes at each $r_i$ and tends to $0$ at $\pm\infty$; by Rolle's theorem (and its version on $(-\infty,r_1]$ and $[r_m,\infty)$ for a nonzero function vanishing at the endpoint and at infinity), $G'$ has a zero in each of the $m+1$ intervals $(-\infty,r_1),(r_1,r_2),\dots,(r_m,\infty)$. So $p_{m+1}$ (degree $m+1$) has $m+1$ distinct real roots, all simple. By induction every $p_m$ has $m$ simple real roots. (These are the Hermite polynomials $He_m$.)

**Conclusion.** Choose $s_0<r_1<s_1<r_2<\dots<r_m<s_m$; because the roots are simple, $p_m(s_0),\dots,p_m(s_m)$ are nonzero with alternating signs. As $H_n(s_i)\to p_m(s_i)$, there is $N$ such that for $n\ge N$ each $H_n(s_i)$ has the sign of $p_m(s_i)$, so $H_n$ has a root in each $(s_{i-1},s_i)$: that is $m$ distinct real roots, i.e. all roots of the degree-$m$ polynomial $H_n$. Since $f_n(x)=n^{m/2}H_n\bigl((x+n)/\sqrt n\bigr)$, all roots of $f_n$ are real for $n\ge N$. ∎

*Remark.* The official solution argues directly: by induction on the degree, $f_n'$ eventually has $m-1$ simple real zeros which interlace from step to step; their minimal spacing never decreases, and from this one shows that the local maxima of $f_n$ tend to $+\infty$ and the local minima to $-\infty$, so eventually $f_n$ has $m$ real zeros.
